1:
The title and the setting are taken four ways. Adam Clarke reports that the Chaldee supposes the psalm composed at the time of the pestilence, when David prayed the Lord not to destroy the people, while some Jewish writers take the title’s opening word for the start of another psalm to whose air this one was sung; he himself thinks it written during the captivity and a continuation of the psalm before, whose abrupt ending the first verse here would properly close. Keil and Delitzsch make the same connection the other way round: what the preceding psalm prays for, this one beholds, and its Asaphic character recalls an earlier psalm of that name. Augustine of Hippo works from the Latin title, corrupt not, and reads it as a plea that God perform what he has promised — but at the end, to which the mind’s eye must be directed, since the felicity of the proud passes like a shadow. John Calvin refuses to spend effort on the author, David or some other prophet, and takes the theme to be that the world is governed wholly by the will of God.

Matthew Henry and C.H. Spurgeon both dwell on the repeated thanksgiving. Henry asks whether, having prayed often for mercy, we should think it enough to give thanks once or twice. Spurgeon calls stinted gratitude ingratitude and asks measureless thanks for infinite goodness, comparing gratitude after God’s smiles to flowers reflecting the colours of the sunbeam. John Calvin observes that the repetition expresses the more forcibly the psalmist’s ardent zeal. Charles Ellicott reads the clause about the name being near as the old conviction, renewed by the wonders just wrought, that the name of God is a word of power to save.

What is received in the second verse divides the entry. Charles Ellicott takes the word in its first derivative sense of a set time, so that the line reads, when I have chosen my time I will judge uprightly, the emphatic pronoun supplying the my; the Greek and Latin agree, though Symmachus gives synagogue. He adds that the speaker here is plainly God himself, breaking in with an announcement of judgment, though how far that utterance extends is unclear, some ending it at the third verse and others at the fifth. John Gill canvasses three senses — the promise, from the Arabic, meaning the gifts of the Spirit; the set time of the world’s judgment, with the versions and the Targum; and the congregation, since Israel met at the door of the tabernacle so named — and settles on the last, making it the church of the firstborn. Adam Clarke and John Wesley keep the congregation but make it Israel, brought back into favour out of captivity or gathered as all the tribes.

The dissolving earth produces four accounts of its pillars. Charles Ellicott would punctuate the verse as question and answer — are earth and all its inhabitants dissolved? it was I who adjusted its pillars — noting that the verb elsewhere means to weigh or measure, so that the sense is to fit the pillars to the weight they must bear, and that the pillars are the mountains, for which he quotes Shelley’s cloud hanging like a roof whose columns are the mountains. Adam Clarke makes them the divine power itself, since all things dissolve when he withdraws it; but he offers a second reading for those who date the psalm before David’s anointing, on which the land is disorganized and the pillars are the expectation of the chief people, fixed on David and alone preventing them from breaking into actual rebellion. John Wesley makes them good magistrates, good ministers and good men, who are indeed the pillars of a nation. John Gill hears the melting of the last day, the inhabitants dissolved through dread of the Judge and the earth by fire.
4:
Charles Ellicott would render the address not to fools but to the arrogant, and not deal foolishly but arrogantly. On the horn he takes the figure from horned animals, a symbol of honour and of strength, and would render the stiff neck as the neck proudly or wantonly raised. John Wesley takes the same metaphor from untamed oxen, which will not bow their heads to receive the yoke, and reads the stiffness as pride and contempt. Adam Clarke supplies a modern observation instead: a traveller had noted that the kings of Abyssinia wear a horn on the diadem, and that keeping it erect or projecting makes them appear as though they had a stiff neck, which Clarke offers as evidence for the antiquity of both the usage and the appearance. John Gill hears the little horn and the beast with ten horns of prophecy, whose look is more stout than his fellows. Adam Clarke reads the warning historically as well, as given to the idolatrous Chaldeans, who were charged not to use their power to oppress and abused it notwithstanding.

The sixth verse breaks off before its own conclusion, and the entry divides over how to finish it. Charles Ellicott observes that the received version rightly sets aside the pointing of the text, which with the Greek and Latin yields a sentence with no conclusion at all; the recurrence of the verb for lifting up in the verses on either side favours reading the disputed word as part of that same verb rather than as the noun mountains, and wilderness may stand for the south. He reports Ewald’s remedy — insert a conjunction, let desert and mountains stand for south and north, and supply the ending from the next verse, so that neither from east nor west nor desert nor mountains cometh judgment, but God is judge — and then declines it, since it is hardly needful to expect such scientific accuracy about the points of the compass in Hebrew poetry.

Adam Clarke answers the same verse with a map. Following Calmet he notes that Babylon had Media, Armenia and Mesopotamia to the east, whence came Darius the Mede, and Arabia, Phoenicia and Egypt to the west, whence came Cyrus who overthrew the Chaldean empire, while by the mountains of the desert Persia may be meant; no help came to the Babylonians from any of those quarters. John Gill reports a reading that makes the words those of the fools themselves, triumphing that no exaltation shall come from any quarter for Christ and his people — a boast in which he says they are mistaken. His own sense is the plain one, that promotion is not from men or from any quarter under heaven, since by God kings reign and he can take away what he gives. Matthew Henry draws the same doctrine and its inference: since kings receive their power from God alone, those were fools who lifted up the horn against David. C.H. Spurgeon adds that men see the human force and the carnal passion but forget the unseen Lord, who is at work behind and within the cloud and already on the way with the cup in his hand.
7:
John Gill reads the seventh verse as the ground of the warning before it — because God is the Judge — and lists the attributes that make the office terrible: omniscient, so that the hidden things of darkness are brought to light and the counsels of the heart made manifest; omnipotent, able to raise the dead and to execute the sentences he passes; omnipresent, so that there is no fleeing from him; and holy and just, rendering to every man according to his works.

The cup in the eighth verse is the most worked-over image in the psalm. Charles Ellicott traces the figure of the cup of divine fury from the more general one that makes life itself a draught to be drunk, bitter or sweet according to the portion assigned, and follows it through the prophets. He would render the wine not red but foaming, from the rapid pouring out, and drain rather than wring; and though the word for mixture may properly mean wine mingled with spices, he thinks it here implies the blending of the portions destined for the good and the bad in Israel, with only the dregs left for the wicked of the earth. The Greek and Latin, he notes, seem to have read a slightly different text — a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, turned from this side to that — which points still more distinctly the same way. John Wesley makes God the master of a feast distributing portions to his guests, with the wine mingled not with water but with strengthening and intoxicating ingredients, and the dregs the worst and most dreadful part of the tribulations, brought on the drinkers by their own choice. Adam Clarke hears something grimmer: an allusion to the stupefying potion given to criminals to drink before their execution. John Gill keeps it plain, as afflictions and judgments measured out in proportion to men’s sins.

Who speaks the ninth verse divides the close. John Gill denies it to the psalmist and gives it to Christ, who on his reading has been speaking all along in this psalm; what is to be declared is left unexpressed and must be supplied — the wonderful works of God, with the Targum, or the judgments to be passed on his enemies, or the name of the Lord with his purposes and covenant. Adam Clarke takes it for the psalmist magnifying God for the promise of deliverance. Keil and Delitzsch read it as the poet turning back from the prophetically presented future to his own present, contrasting himself as a member of the still oppressed church with its proud oppressors, and finding in the words for ever a promise that for one who gives himself so entirely to God the Redeemer there is no dying. C.H. Spurgeon sets two choirs against each other, the saints chanting while their foes roar in anguish over the wrath-wine. On the horns of the last verse John Gill hears the ten horns of prophecy and reports that Jewish interpreters take them for the horns of the nations, one of them meaning by the horns of Esau the Roman empire; C.H. Spurgeon notes that men then wore horns as part of their state, so that the lopping is both literal and figurative; John Wesley refers the cutting to the time when the speaker is advanced to the throne; and Adam Clarke reports the whole punctually fulfilled, the Babylonians cut off and the Jews delivered and exalted.
